claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by a fine, uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Nanoscale precipitates obstruct crack propagation and promote plastic energy dissipation.
Thermal treatments that coarsen the precipitates cause a loss of toughness.
The proposed initial state is a rapidly solidified, fine-grained FCC or dual-phase high-entropy alloy with a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates.
Increasing annealing temperature and duration will promote precipitate coarsening while overall composition and phase constitution remain unchanged.
The proposed annealing range is approximately 800–1100°C for 1, 5, and 10 hours in argon.
Precipitate size, precipitate spatial distribution, and grain-boundary characteristics mediate the toughness response.
Fine nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Fine nanoscale precipitates promote crack deflection and local plastic deformation, thereby enhancing toughness.
Coarsened precipitates become stress-concentration sites that facilitate crack initiation and propagation.
Relative to the rapidly solidified baseline, treatments producing greater precipitate coarsening will produce progressively lower impact toughness.
The proposed behavior is expected in high-entropy alloys whose toughness depends on precipitate strengthening and microstructural heterogeneity.
The proposed behavior may not apply when a uniform single-phase FCC structure or transformation-induced plasticity dominates toughness.
A lack of toughness reduction, or an increase in toughness, despite significant annealing-induced precipitate coarsening would falsify the proposed mechanism.
